doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Open chords versus real changes; learning on the job
summary: Family playing used only open chords; Pallo says he learned more on gigs from better and even lesser players than from lessons, and dependability matters.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: No not just Italian but the standards and if they did play standards they didn’t use all of the right chords, if you were playing all open chords, so instead of like using a C to a C diminished or a C sharp diminished to the D minor seventh to a G seventh, you would just play C and a G seven. You know, it would sound okay. It would.
Sure. And the spirit was there.
How much in your guitar lessons over the years was valuable for when you started playing gigs? Let me rephrase that.
Was there a lot of learning on the job for you?

That’s what I was going to get at, yes. Learning was on the job training, let’s put it that way. You learn more playing with better musicians, that’s number one, and you learn more that way than you can taking lessons. I mean taking lessons of course gives you the basic. But then once you’re on a gig — as we call it, the gig — you’ll see what one person has that you don’t do and you’ll pick up what he has and you’ll see what the trumpet player’s doing or the pianist or whatever, and it’s better that way. That’s what I was going to get at when you asked that question.

Also on a gig is there a certain amount, for a young player, not learning only what and how to play but how to act? How to comport yourself? How to be a professional? Like you know, you don’t necessarily hire the best player, you also hire people who are dependable.

Yes. That’s another thing to talk about. Yes. Maybe less of a musician but more dependable as you said. Sometimes that’s even better. And so actually you learn from all of them, every one of them, and even from a lesser player, he might do something that you can pick up ideas from. There’s always different ideas. I’ve heard standards where like we were talking about difference in changes and chords where you can, it comes back real smooth and so forth. A fellow who doesn’t use that might come up with something, you say whoa, that sounded great, I think I’ll try that. And you try it and then you could fit it in with yours and add it into your repertoire.
